column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Which subatomic particle carries a positive (+) charge?
column28: Protons are the positive particles in the nucleus. Electrons are negative and neutrons have no charge. The nucleus is not a particle; it is the center of the atom where protons and neutrons are found.
column29: Think of the word positive. Which particle name also starts with "p"?

column9: Match each subatomic particle to its electric charge.
column28: Protons are positive, electrons are negative, and neutrons are neutral (no charge). A common mistake is mixing up protons and neutrons; remember neutron sounds like neutral.
column29: Neutron sounds like neutral.

column9: In a Bohr model drawing of an atom, the rings drawn around the center show the energy levels of which particles?
column28: Electrons move around the nucleus in energy levels, which the Bohr model draws as rings. Protons and neutrons stay packed together in the nucleus at the center.
column29: Which particle is found outside the nucleus?

column9: The small, dense, positively charged center of an atom is called the ___.
column28: The nucleus is the center of the atom. It holds the protons (+) and neutrons (0), so its overall charge is positive. Electrons are outside the nucleus, not in it.
column29: It holds the protons and neutrons.

column9: Phosphorus has an atomic number of 15. How many protons are in every phosphorus atom?
column28: The atomic number is the number of protons, so every phosphorus atom has 15 protons. A common mistake is adding or subtracting other numbers; the atomic number IS the proton count.
column29: What does the atomic number count?

column9: Which of these substances is an element?
column28: Copper is made of only one kind of atom (Cu), so it is an element. Water, salt, and baking soda each contain two or more different elements bonded together, so they are compounds.
column29: Look at each formula. Which one has only ONE kind of element symbol?

column9: Which element is one of the six most common elements in living things and is found in DNA, ATP, and cell membranes?
column28: Phosphorus (P) is part of DNA, ATP, and the phospholipids in cell membranes. Potassium, sodium, and iron are important to the body, but they are not among the six most common elements (carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, sulfur).
column29: Think about the "phospho" in phospholipid.

column9: Nitrogen is one of the six most common elements in living things. Nitrogen is especially important in which molecules?
column16: None; nitrogen is only found in the air
column28: Nitrogen is part of every amino acid (the building blocks of proteins) and every DNA base. Water and salt contain no nitrogen. Air is mostly nitrogen gas, but living things also build nitrogen into their molecules.
column29: What macromolecules are built from amino acids and nucleotides?

column9: Your nerve cells send signals using potassium ions, written K⁺. What does the + sign tell you about a K⁺ ion?
column28: An ion becomes positive when it loses electrons, because it then has more protons than electrons. A common mistake is thinking it gained a proton; changing protons would make a different element.
column29: Ions form when atoms gain or lose the negative particles.

column9: Two hydrogen atoms, each with 1 electron, join to make one H₂ molecule by sharing their electrons. How many electrons are shared between the two atoms?
column28: Each hydrogen brings 1 electron, so together they share 1 pair = 2 electrons. That shared pair is one single covalent bond. A common mistake is answering 1.
column29: Add up the electrons both atoms bring to the bond.

column9: In an ionic bond, what holds the two ions together?
column17: A weak attraction between water molecules
column28: In an ionic bond one atom transfers electrons to the other. The positive ion and the negative ion then attract each other because opposite charges attract. Sharing electrons describes a covalent bond.
column29: One ion is positive and one is negative. What do opposite charges do?

column9: Match each term to its meaning.
column14: Atom :: The smallest unit of matter that keeps an element's properties
column15: Element :: A pure substance made of only one kind of atom
column16: Molecule :: Two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds
column17: Compound :: Two or more different elements bonded in a fixed ratio
column28: An atom is the smallest unit; an element is one kind of atom; a molecule is atoms bonded together; a compound must contain different elements. The common mix-up is molecule vs. compound: a compound needs at least two DIFFERENT elements.
column29: The word DIFFERENT is the key to one of these.

column9: Match each type of bond to its description.
column14: Ionic bond :: Electrons are transferred from one atom to another
column15: Covalent bond :: Electrons are shared between atoms
column16: Hydrogen bond :: A weak attraction between molecules
column28: Ionic = transfer, covalent = share, hydrogen bond = a weak attraction between molecules (like water sticking to water). Students often swap ionic and covalent; co-valent sounds like co-operate, which means share.
column29: Co-valent, like co-worker: they share.

column9: Protons and electrons have about the same mass.
column28: False. A proton is about 1,800 times heavier than an electron. Protons and neutrons give an atom almost all of its mass; electrons add very little. Students often assume equal charge size means equal mass.
column29: Equal charge (+1 and −1) does not mean equal size.

column9: Hydrogen bonds are stronger than the covalent bonds that hold the atoms of a water molecule together.
column28: False. Covalent bonds are strong and hold atoms together inside a molecule. Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between molecules. That is why water molecules can slide past each other but each molecule stays H₂O.
column29: Which bond is described as weak?

column9: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are atoms of two different elements.
column28: False. Both have 6 protons, so both are carbon. They are isotopes: they differ only in their number of neutrons (6 vs. 8). The number of protons, not the mass, decides the element.
column29: What do both names start with, and what decides an element?

column9: Atoms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons are called ___.
column28: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they have different masses. Don't confuse them with ions, which have a different number of electrons.
column29: It is NOT ion. Ions are about electrons.

column9: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom is called its ___ number.
column28: The atomic number is the number of protons, and it tells you which element the atom is. The mass number is a different number: protons plus neutrons.
column29: This number is printed above each symbol on the periodic table.

column9: A neutral atom of one of the six main elements of life has 7 electrons. Which element is it?
column28: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. 7 electrons means 7 protons, and the element with 7 protons is nitrogen. A common mistake is thinking electrons and protons do not have to match in a neutral atom.
column29: In a neutral atom, electrons = protons.

column9: In the formula CO₂, what does the small 2 mean?
column28: A subscript tells how many atoms of the element right before it are in the molecule. The 2 follows O, so there are 2 oxygen atoms and 1 carbon atom. Students often apply the subscript to the wrong element.
column29: A subscript belongs to the symbol written just before it.

column9: Hair and fingernails are made of the protein keratin, which contains a lot of the element with the symbol S. Which element is it?
column28: S is the symbol for sulfur, one of the six most common elements in living things; it is found in some proteins. Sodium's symbol is Na, silicon is Si, and selenium is Se.
column29: It is the last letter of CHNOPS.

column9: Toothpaste contains fluoride ions, F⁻. How did a fluorine atom become an F⁻ ion?
column17: It shared electrons with another fluorine atom
column28: Gaining a negative electron gives the atom one more electron than protons, so it becomes −1. Losing an electron would make it positive. A common mistake is thinking the − sign means something was lost.
column29: A negative charge means extra negative particles.

column9: Biology builds from small to big. Put these levels in order from smallest to largest.
column28: Atoms bond to make small molecules like glucose; many glucose molecules link to make a macromolecule like starch; and cells are built from huge numbers of macromolecules. A common slip is putting the molecule before the atom.
column29: Atoms build molecules. Molecules build macromolecules.

column9: Select every substance that is a compound. Select all that apply.
column28: Ammonia, potassium chloride, and hydrogen peroxide each contain two different elements bonded together, so they are compounds. Ozone is three oxygen atoms (one element), and zinc and helium are single elements. A common mistake is calling O₃ a compound because it has more than one atom.
column29: Count the different element symbols in each formula. A compound needs at least two.

column9: Which particles do atoms use when they form chemical bonds?
column28: Chemical bonds form when electrons are shared (covalent) or transferred (ionic). Protons and neutrons stay in the nucleus and do not take part in bonding.
column29: Which particle is on the outside of the atom, where atoms touch?

column9: A normal oxygen atom has no overall charge. Why?
column14: It has the same number of protons and electrons
column15: It has the same number of protons and neutrons
column17: Its neutrons cancel out the charge of its protons
column28: Each proton (+1) is balanced by an electron (−1), so equal numbers cancel out. Neutrons have no charge, so they cannot cancel anything. That neutron idea is the most common mistake.
column29: Which two particles have opposite charges?

column9: Baking soda has the formula NaHCO₃. How many different elements are in baking soda?
column28: The symbols are Na (sodium), H (hydrogen), C (carbon), and O (oxygen): 4 different elements. A common mistake is counting atoms (6) instead of different elements, or reading Na as two elements.
column29: A capital letter starts each new element symbol.

column9: Which type of bond links the carbon atoms together in the long chains of sugars and fats?
column16: No bonds; the atoms just sit next to each other
column28: Carbon atoms share electrons with each other, forming strong covalent bonds. Covalent bonds build every molecule in the body. Ionic bonds involve transferring electrons to form ions, and hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between molecules.
column29: Carbon atoms don't give electrons away; they share them.

column9: Sports drinks advertise "electrolytes" such as Na⁺ and K⁺. What kind of particles are Na⁺ and K⁺?
column28: The + sign shows a charge, and a charged atom is an ion. Isotopes differ in neutrons and are not charged. Na⁺ and K⁺ are single atoms, so they are not molecules.
column29: What does the + sign show?

column9: Hydrogen and oxygen are both gases at room temperature, but water (H₂O), which is made from them, is a liquid. What does this show?
column14: Hydrogen and oxygen turn into a new element when they bond
column15: A compound can have very different properties than the elements it is made of
column16: Water is not really a compound, because hydrogen and oxygen are only mixed together in it
column17: Compounds always keep the same properties as the elements that were used to make them
column28: When elements bond to form a compound, the compound has its own new properties. The elements themselves don't change into new elements; they are still hydrogen and oxygen atoms, just bonded together.
column29: Are the properties of water the same as the gases it came from?

column9: Which statements about electrons are true? Select all that apply.
column14: They are much heavier than protons
column16: They are packed inside the nucleus with the neutrons
column17: They move around the nucleus in energy levels
column18: They are the particles involved in chemical bonds
column28: Electrons are negative, move in energy levels around the nucleus, and form chemical bonds. They are much LIGHTER than protons and are found outside the nucleus.
column29: Two of these are false. Electrons are tiny and live outside the nucleus.

column9: Table salt has the formula NaCl. Which two elements are bonded in table salt?
column28: Na is the symbol for sodium and Cl is chlorine. A common mistake is reading Na as nitrogen (N) or Cl as carbon (C); a two-letter symbol is one element.
column29: Na comes from the Latin name for sodium.

column9: In a Bohr model, what is the greatest number of electrons the first energy level (closest to the nucleus) can hold?
column28: The first energy level holds at most 2 electrons. The next levels can hold 8 each for the atoms in biology. A common mistake is answering 8.
column29: Hydrogen and helium fill only this first level.

column9: A party balloon is filled with helium, which exists as single He atoms that do not bond. How should helium be described?
column14: An element made of single, unbonded atoms
column15: A compound, because the helium atoms are bonded to each other
column16: A molecule made of two elements
column17: A negative ion that has gained extra electrons
column28: Helium is one kind of atom, so it is an element. Its atoms do not bond, so it is not a molecule or compound. It has no charge, so it is not an ion.
column29: Does helium contain more than one kind of atom, and are its atoms bonded?

column9: Glucose has the formula C₆H₁₂O₆. Which elements make up glucose?
column28: C is carbon, H is hydrogen, and O is oxygen. Calcium (Ca), helium (He), copper (Cu), and osmium (Os) all have two-letter symbols.
column29: Each one-capital-letter symbol is one element.

column9: Which pair of ions would be attracted to each other and form an ionic bond?
column28: Ionic bonds form between a positive ion and a negative ion, because opposite charges attract. Two positive ions (or two negative ions) repel each other.
column29: Opposites attract; like charges push apart.

column9: Match each term to the best example.
column15: Isotope :: Deuterium, a heavier form of hydrogen
column16: Element :: A bar of pure gold, Au
column28: Na⁺ has a charge, so it is an ion. Deuterium is hydrogen with an extra neutron, so it is an isotope. Gold is one kind of atom, an element. Sugar has three different elements bonded, a compound. The common mix-up is ion vs. isotope: charge means ion, different mass means isotope.
column29: Look for a charge sign, a heavier form, one symbol, and a mix of symbols.

column9: Most of an atom's space (volume) is taken up by
column14: The nucleus, because it holds all of the protons and neutrons
column16: The region around the nucleus where electrons move
column17: The neutrons packed together in the center
column28: The nucleus is tiny compared to the whole atom. Almost all of an atom's volume is the space where the electrons move. Students often confuse mass with space: the nucleus has most of the MASS, but very little of the space.
column29: Mass and space are not the same thing.

column9: What does a chemical formula, such as H₂O, tell you?
column14: The shape and color of one molecule of the substance
column15: Which elements are in the substance and how many atoms of each
column16: How much the substance weighs in grams
column17: Whether the substance is a solid, liquid, or gas at room temperature
column28: A chemical formula lists the element symbols and uses subscripts to show how many atoms of each are in one unit. It does not tell the color, state, or weight of a sample.
column29: Look at what is actually written in H₂O: letters and small numbers.

column9: Select every particle that is an ion. Select all that apply.
column28: An ion is an atom with a charge, shown by a + or − sign. Zn²⁺, Cl⁻, and Fe³⁺ all carry a charge. CO₂, He, and H₂O have no charge sign. Don't mistake the small subscript numbers in CO₂ and H₂O for charges.
column29: Look for a + or − in the top right corner.

column9: Your body needs calcium for bones, iron for blood, and iodine for the thyroid gland. Calcium, iron, and iodine are all
column28: Each one is a single kind of atom, so each is an element. Compounds and molecules are made of atoms bonded together. Isotopes are versions of one element with different neutrons.
column29: Each has its own box on the periodic table.

column9: The number of protons plus the number of neutrons in an atom is its ___ number.
column28: Mass number = protons + neutrons, because those two particles make up almost all of an atom's mass. The atomic number counts only the protons. Electrons are too light to count.
column29: Protons and neutrons are the heavy particles.

column9: Iodized salt contains potassium iodide, KI. What does the formula KI tell you?
column14: It has 1 krypton for every 1 iodine
column15: It has 1 potassium for every 1 iron
column16: It has 1 potassium for every 1 iodine
column17: It is a single element called KI
column28: K is the symbol for potassium and I is iodine. With no subscripts, the ratio is 1 to 1. Krypton is Kr and iron is Fe. KI has two capital letters, so it has two elements and is a compound.
column29: No subscript means 1. Two capital letters means two elements.

column9: Counting by number of atoms, which element is the most common in the human body?
column28: Hydrogen is the most common atom in the body, because water (H₂O) and nearly every organic molecule contain lots of hydrogen. Carbon is the backbone of the large molecules, but there are fewer carbon atoms than hydrogen atoms.
column29: Your body is mostly water. Which atom does water have two of?

column9: Caffeine has the formula C₈H₁₀N₄O₂. How many nitrogen atoms are in one caffeine molecule?
column28: The subscript right after N is 4, so there are 4 nitrogen atoms. A common mistake is reading the number before the symbol instead of after it.
column29: Find N, then read the small number right after it.

column9: An oxygen atom has 8 protons and 10 neutrons. What is its mass number?
column28: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 8 + 10 = 18. This is oxygen-18. A common mistake is adding the electrons too, or answering 8 (the atomic number).
column29: Add the two particles found in the nucleus.

column9: A nitrogen-15 atom has 7 protons. How many neutrons does it have?
column28: The 15 in nitrogen-15 is the mass number (protons + neutrons). Neutrons = 15 − 7 = 8. A common mistake is adding 15 + 7 or answering 7.
column29: The number in the name is protons plus neutrons.

column9: Table sugar (sucrose) has the formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. How many atoms in total are in one sucrose molecule?
column28: Add the subscripts: 12 carbon + 22 hydrogen + 11 oxygen = 45 atoms. A common mistake is counting the 3 elements instead of the atoms.
column29: Add up all three subscripts.

column9: Many enzymes need zinc ions, Zn²⁺, to work. A zinc atom has 30 protons. How many electrons does a Zn²⁺ ion have?
column28: The 2+ charge means the atom lost 2 electrons. A neutral zinc atom has 30 electrons, so Zn²⁺ has 30 − 2 = 28. A common mistake is adding 2 (32), which would make a negative ion.
column29: A + charge means electrons were lost.

column9: Four particles are described below. Which one is a neutral atom?
column28: A neutral atom has equal protons and electrons: 19 and 19. The number of neutrons does not affect charge. The others have more or fewer electrons than protons, so they are ions. A common mistake is comparing protons to neutrons.
column29: Ignore the neutrons; they have no charge.

column9: Select every substance that is a molecule but NOT a compound. Select all that apply.
column28: O₃, H₂, and F₂ are two or more atoms bonded together (molecules) but contain only one element, so they are not compounds. H₂O and CO contain two different elements, so they are compounds. Argon atoms are single and unbonded, so argon is not a molecule.
column29: First check: is there more than one atom bonded? Then: is there more than one kind of element?

column9: The structural formula for water is drawn as H–O–H. What does each line (–) represent?
column14: An ionic bond, where an electron is transferred from H to O
column15: A covalent bond, which is a shared pair of electrons
column16: A hydrogen bond between two water molecules
column17: A neutron that connects the atoms
column28: In a structural formula each line is a covalent bond: one pair of shared electrons. The atoms inside a water molecule share electrons. Hydrogen bonds happen between separate water molecules, not inside one.
column29: The line connects atoms inside ONE molecule.

column9: Two chlorine atoms each need one more electron to fill their outer shell. Neither atom can pull an electron away from the other, so they join to make Cl₂. What type of bond forms?
column28: When two atoms pull equally, neither can take an electron, so they share a pair. Sharing is a covalent bond. An ionic bond needs one atom to give an electron away.
column29: If neither one can take an electron, what is the other way to get one?

column9: Magnesium gives 2 electrons to an oxygen atom to make magnesium oxide, MgO. What are the charges on the two ions?
column28: Magnesium loses 2 electrons, so it becomes 2+. Oxygen gains those 2 electrons, so it becomes 2−. A common mistake is flipping the signs; losing negative electrons makes an atom positive.
column29: Losing negative particles leaves an atom positive.

column9: A sulfur atom (16 protons) gains 2 electrons. What is the charge of the ion?
column28: After gaining 2 electrons, sulfur has 18 electrons and 16 protons, so it has 2 extra negative charges: 2−. Gaining electrons always makes an ion more negative.
column29: Compare 16 protons with the new number of electrons.

column9: Nitrogen-14 and nitrogen-15 both bond with hydrogen to make ammonia in exactly the same way. Why do isotopes of an element have the same chemistry?
column14: They have the same number of neutrons in the nucleus
column16: They have the same number of protons and electrons
column17: They are actually the same isotope with two different names
column28: Chemistry depends on electrons, and the number of electrons in a neutral atom matches the number of protons. Isotopes have the same protons (and electrons) but different neutrons and different masses.
column29: Which particles take part in bonding?

column9: Match each substance to the description that fits it best.
column14: N₂ (nitrogen gas) :: A molecule made of only one element
column15: H₂S (the gas that smells like rotten eggs) :: A molecule that is also a compound
column16: KCl (potassium chloride) :: A compound made of ions
column28: N₂ has two nitrogen atoms bonded, so it is a molecule but not a compound. H₂S has two different elements sharing electrons, so it is a molecule and a compound. KCl is potassium (metal) bonded to chlorine by an ionic bond, so it is a compound made of ions.
column29: Ask two questions: how many different elements? Shared or transferred electrons?

column9: Put these molecules in order from the fewest total atoms to the most.
column28: H₂ has 2 atoms, H₂O has 3, NH₃ has 4, and C₂H₆O has 2 + 6 + 1 = 9. A common mistake is forgetting that a symbol with no subscript still counts as 1 atom.
column29: Add up the subscripts; a symbol with no number counts as 1.

column9: A beaker contains 3 molecules of water, written 3 H₂O. How many atoms in total are in these 3 molecules?
column28: One H₂O has 3 atoms (2 H + 1 O). Three molecules have 3 × 3 = 9 atoms. A common mistake is answering 3 (counting molecules) or 6 (counting only hydrogen).
column29: Count the atoms in one molecule first, then multiply.

column9: Water is always H₂O, with 2 hydrogen atoms for every 1 oxygen atom. Hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂, is a different substance that bleaches hair. What does this show about compounds?
column14: H₂O₂ is just water with an extra oxygen atom mixed in, not bonded to it
column15: The ratio of elements in a compound does not matter, as long as the elements are the same
column16: H₂O₂ must be an element because it has extra oxygen
column17: A compound has a fixed ratio of elements; a new ratio makes a new substance
column28: Every compound has its own fixed ratio of elements. H₂O and H₂O₂ have the same elements in different ratios, so they are different compounds with different properties. The extra oxygen is bonded in, not mixed in.
column29: Same elements, different numbers. Same substance or not?

column9: Ionic bonds usually form between a metal and a nonmetal. Select every substance held together by ionic bonds. Select all that apply.
column28: K, Ca, and Na are metals that give electrons to the nonmetals I, Cl, and F, forming ionic bonds. NH₃, CO₂, and glucose contain only nonmetals, which share electrons in covalent bonds. A common mistake is thinking anything called a "salt" or anything that dissolves must be ionic; check the elements.
column29: Look for a metal (left side of the periodic table) at the start of the formula.

column9: Hydrogen forms only 1 covalent bond, and oxygen usually forms 2. Which structural formula for hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is drawn correctly?
column28: In H–O–O–H each H has 1 bond and each O has 2 bonds. In the other drawings a hydrogen is in the middle with 2 bonds, which hydrogen cannot do. A common mistake is ignoring how many bonds each atom can make.
column29: Count the lines touching each H. It should be exactly one.

column9: Why do atoms form chemical bonds?
column14: To gain more protons so the nucleus becomes larger
column15: To become more stable by filling their outer energy level
column16: To turn into a different element that has a full set of protons
column28: Atoms bond to become stable, usually by filling their outer energy level with electrons. They do this by sharing or transferring electrons. Bonding never changes the number of protons, so the atom stays the same element.
column29: Bonds involve electrons. What are atoms trying to fill?

column9: A hydrogen bond forms when a slightly positive hydrogen atom is attracted to a slightly negative atom of which elements?
column28: Hydrogen bonds form between a slightly positive H and a slightly negative O or N, like in water and between the bases of DNA. Carbon does not pull hard enough on electrons, and sodium, potassium, helium, and neon do not form hydrogen bonds.
column29: Think of water (H₂O) and the bases of DNA, which contain nitrogen.

column9: Put the steps in order to show how potassium and chlorine form potassium chloride, KCl.
column14: The K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions attract each other because of their opposite charges
column15: A potassium atom gives one electron to a chlorine atom
column16: Potassium becomes K⁺ and chlorine becomes Cl⁻
column28: First the electron is transferred, which turns the atoms into ions with opposite charges, and then the opposite charges attract to form the ionic bond. A common mistake is putting the attraction first; atoms are neutral until the electron moves.
column29: The atoms have no charge until something moves.

column9: In a model, atom X loses an electron and atom Y gains that electron. The two then stick together. Which statement describes the result?
column14: X is a negative ion, Y is a positive ion, and they are held by an ionic bond
column15: Both atoms are still neutral and share electrons in a covalent bond
column16: X is a positive ion, Y is a negative ion, and they are held by an ionic bond
column17: X and Y share a pair of electrons, so it is a hydrogen bond
column28: Losing an electron makes X positive; gaining one makes Y negative. A transfer of electrons followed by attraction is an ionic bond. The most common mistake is reversing which ion is positive.
column29: Losing negative charge leaves something positive.

column9: Your red blood cells need iron, which has atomic number 26. Which statement about a sample of pure iron is true?
column14: Every atom in the sample has 26 protons
column15: It contains at least two different kinds of atoms
column16: It is a compound because it has many atoms
column28: Pure iron is an element, so every atom is iron, and every iron atom has 26 protons. Having many atoms does not make something a compound; a compound needs different elements bonded together.
column29: What does the atomic number tell you about EVERY atom of an element?

column9: In an unsaturated fat, some carbon atoms are joined by a double bond, C=C. How many electrons are shared in one double bond?
column28: A single bond is one shared pair (2 electrons). A double bond is two shared pairs: 2 × 2 = 4 electrons. A common mistake is answering 2 because the bond is drawn with two lines.
column29: Each line in the bond stands for one pair of electrons.

column9: Ocean water contains both oxygen-16 and oxygen-18 atoms. Which statement compares them correctly?
column14: Oxygen-18 has 2 more protons than oxygen-16
column15: Oxygen-18 has 2 more electrons than oxygen-16
column16: They are different elements because their masses differ
column17: Oxygen-18 has 2 more neutrons than oxygen-16
column28: Both are oxygen, so both have 8 protons. Their mass numbers differ by 2, so oxygen-18 has 10 neutrons and oxygen-16 has 8. A common mistake is thinking a change in mass means a change in protons, which would make a new element.
column29: Same element means same protons. What is left to change the mass?

column9: Carbon dioxide, CO₂, is the gas you breathe out. Which statements about CO₂ are true? Select all that apply.
column14: It is made of three different elements
column17: It is an element because it is a gas
column18: Its atoms are held together by covalent bonds
column28: CO₂ has carbon and oxygen bonded together (a compound), its atoms are bonded into a unit (a molecule), and the nonmetals share electrons (covalent). It has 3 atoms but only 2 different elements. Being a gas has nothing to do with being an element.
column29: Count atoms and count different elements separately.

column9: The amino acid glycine has the formula C₂H₅NO₂. Glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆. Which element is found in glycine but NOT in glucose?
column28: Both formulas have C, H, and O. Only glycine has N (nitrogen). That nitrogen is a sign of an amino acid; proteins contain nitrogen, while sugars do not.
column29: List the symbols in each formula and compare.

column9: Which pair of atoms are isotopes of the same element?
column14: 6 protons and 6 neutrons; 7 protons and 6 neutrons
column15: 6 protons and 6 neutrons; 6 protons and 7 neutrons
column16: 8 protons and 8 neutrons; 7 protons and 8 neutrons
column17: 6 protons, 6 neutrons, 6 electrons; 6 protons, 6 neutrons, 4 electrons
column28: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. The pair with 6 protons each but 6 and 7 neutrons fits. Pairs with different protons are different elements. The last pair differs only in electrons, which makes an atom and an ion, not isotopes.
column29: Same protons, different neutrons.

column9: Match each particle to its overall charge.
column28: Charge = protons − electrons. 8 − 8 = 0, 19 − 18 = +1, 9 − 10 = −1, and 12 − 10 = +2. A common mistake is getting the sign backwards; more electrons than protons means negative.
column29: Subtract electrons from protons.

column9: Which statement about carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur is true?
column16: They are found only in living things, not in rocks, air, or water
column17: Together they make up about 99% of the mass of living things
column28: These six elements (CHNOPS) make up about 99% of living things. They are all nonmetals, and they are elements, not compounds. They are also found in non-living things, like rocks, air, and water.
column29: Are these single elements or combinations? Are they only in living things?

column9: Rank these by size, starting with the smallest.
column15: The nucleus of a carbon atom
column28: A proton is one of the 12 particles in a carbon nucleus; the nucleus is a tiny part of the whole carbon atom; and glucose is built from 24 atoms, including 6 carbon atoms. A common mistake is thinking the nucleus is as large as the atom.
column29: Each item on the list is part of the next bigger one.

column9: When water boils, the molecules separate from each other and float off as steam, but each molecule is still H₂O. Which bonds break when water boils?
column15: Covalent bonds inside each water molecule
column16: Ionic bonds between hydrogen and oxygen
column17: Bonds inside the nucleus of each atom
column28: Steam is still H₂O, so the strong covalent bonds inside each molecule did not break. Only the weak hydrogen bonds between molecules broke. A common mistake is thinking boiling splits water into hydrogen and oxygen.
column29: If the covalent bonds broke, would the steam still be H₂O?

column9: When a cell copies its DNA, the two strands of the double helix unzip from each other, but each strand stays in one piece. Which statement best explains this?
column14: The strands are held to each other by strong covalent bonds, while each strand is held together by weak hydrogen bonds
column15: Both the strands and the atoms within them are held by ionic bonds
column16: The strands are held to each other by weak hydrogen bonds, while the atoms within each strand are joined by strong covalent bonds
column17: DNA has no chemical bonds, so the strands can easily separate
column28: Weak hydrogen bonds between the bases let the two strands separate easily. Strong covalent bonds hold the atoms of each strand together, so each strand stays whole. A common mistake is reversing the two bond types.
column29: Which bond type is weak enough to "unzip"?

column9: A student writes, "An ion is an atom that has gained or lost protons." What is the best correction?
column14: Ions form by gaining or losing neutrons, since neutrons change how much charge the atom has
column16: Ions form only when two atoms share electrons equally in a covalent bond
column17: Ions form by gaining or losing electrons; changing protons would make a new element
column28: Ions form when electrons are gained or lost. The number of protons defines the element, so changing protons would make a different element, not an ion. Changing neutrons makes an isotope, and sharing electrons is covalent bonding.
column29: What happens to an atom's identity if its protons change?

column9: Particle 1 has 20 protons, 20 neutrons, and 18 electrons. Particle 2 has 20 protons, 22 neutrons, and 20 electrons. Which statement is correct?
column14: They are different elements because they have different numbers of neutrons
column15: Particle 1 is a 2− ion, and particle 2 is a neutral atom
column16: Both are calcium; particle 1 is a 2+ ion, and particle 2 is a neutral atom of a heavier isotope
column17: Both are neutral atoms of the same isotope
column28: Both have 20 protons, so both are the same element (calcium). Particle 1 has 2 fewer electrons than protons, so it is 2+. Particle 2 has equal protons and electrons (neutral) and 2 extra neutrons, so it is a heavier isotope (mass 42 vs. 40). A common mistake is letting neutrons decide the element.
column29: Check protons for identity, electrons for charge, neutrons for mass.

column9: Iodine-131 is a radioactive isotope used to treat thyroid disease. Iodine's atomic number is 53. How many neutrons are in one iodine-131 atom?
column28: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 131 − 53 = 78. A common mistake is adding the numbers (184) or answering 53.
column29: 131 is protons plus neutrons.

column9: The enzyme catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide: 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂. How many oxygen atoms in total are on the right side of the arrow?
column28: 2 H₂O has 2 × 1 = 2 oxygen atoms, and O₂ has 2 more: 2 + 2 = 4. That matches the 4 oxygen atoms in 2 H₂O₂, because atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed. A common mistake is ignoring the 2 in front of H₂O.
column29: A big number in front multiplies the whole molecule.

column9: A normal oxygen atom has 8 protons, 8 neutrons, and 8 electrons. Which changes would turn it into a different isotope of oxygen? Select all that apply.
column28: Changing only the neutrons changes the mass but keeps 8 protons, so it is still oxygen: a new isotope. Adding a proton makes a new element (fluorine). Adding or removing electrons makes an ion, not an isotope.
column29: Isotope means a new mass, same element.

column9: Atom A is a metal with 1 electron in its outer energy level. Atom B is a nonmetal with 7 electrons in its outer energy level, and it needs 8 to be full. What is most likely to happen when they meet?
column14: A and B share one pair of electrons in a covalent bond, so both outer levels fill
column15: A gives its 1 electron to B, and the two ions are held by an ionic bond
column17: They push each other away because both have electrons, so no bond forms
column28: It is far easier for A to lose 1 electron than gain 7, and B only needs 1 more. So A transfers its electron to B, A becomes positive, B becomes negative, and they attract: an ionic bond. Sodium and chlorine behave this way.
column29: Which is easier for each atom: losing or gaining?

column9: Each oxygen atom has 6 outer electrons and needs 8. How do two oxygen atoms bond to make O₂, the oxygen you breathe?
column14: They share two pairs of electrons in a double covalent bond
column15: One oxygen gives 2 electrons to the other in an ionic bond
column16: They share one pair of electrons in a single covalent bond
column17: They are held together by a hydrogen bond
column28: Each oxygen needs 2 more electrons. By sharing two pairs (4 electrons total), both atoms count 8. That is a double covalent bond, O=O. One shared pair would only give each atom 7, and two identical atoms can't transfer electrons to make an ionic bond.
column29: How many electrons is each oxygen short? Each shared pair adds one to each atom's count.

column9: In ammonia, NH₃, the nitrogen atom forms a single covalent bond with each of three hydrogen atoms. How many electrons are shared in total in these bonds?
column28: Each single bond is one shared pair (2 electrons). Three bonds × 2 = 6 electrons. A common mistake is answering 3 (counting bonds) instead of electrons.
column29: Count bonds first, then electrons per bond.

column9: In a lab, a sugar cube is heated in a test tube. It turns into black carbon, and droplets of water form near the top of the tube. What does this show about sugar?
column15: Sugar is made only of carbon, and the water came from the air in the tube
column16: Sugar is a compound that contains carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen
column17: Heating created new elements in the tube that were not in the sugar to begin with
column28: Heating broke the sugar apart into carbon and water. Water contains hydrogen and oxygen, so the sugar must have contained carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen bonded together: a compound. Heating cannot create new elements; it only rearranges the atoms already there.
column29: Where did the hydrogen and oxygen in the water droplets come from?

column9: Passing electricity through water splits it: 2 H₂O → 2 H₂ + O₂. If 10 water molecules are split, how many O₂ molecules can form?
column28: 10 water molecules contain 10 oxygen atoms. Each O₂ needs 2 oxygen atoms, so 10 ÷ 2 = 5 O₂ molecules. (They also make 10 H₂.) A common mistake is answering 10 by assuming one O₂ per water molecule.
column29: Count the oxygen atoms first. How many does each O₂ use?

column9: Why can carbon form the long chains and rings found in sugars, fats, proteins, and DNA?
column14: Each carbon atom can form 4 covalent bonds, to other carbons and to other atoms
column15: Carbon forms ionic bonds with every element
column16: Carbon atoms have no electrons, so they can fit tightly together in long chains
column17: Carbon is a metal that gives away electrons
column28: Carbon has 4 outer electrons and forms 4 covalent bonds. That lets it link to other carbons in chains or rings and still bond to H, O, N, and others. Carbon shares electrons; it does not form ionic bonds with everything, and it is a nonmetal.
column29: How many outer electrons does carbon have to share?

column9: Match each part of a living thing to the type of bond most responsible for holding it together.
column14: Amino acids linked into a protein chain (peptide bonds) :: Covalent bonds
column15: The coils of a protein's α-helix shape :: Hydrogen bonds
column16: K⁺ and Cl⁻ in a crystal of salt substitute :: Ionic bonds
column28: Peptide bonds are covalent bonds linking amino acids. The coils and sheets of a protein's secondary structure are held by weak hydrogen bonds. Oppositely charged K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are held by ionic bonds. A common mistake is thinking a peptide bond is its own type separate from covalent.
column29: Charges point to ionic; a chain of atoms points to covalent; a shape held by weak attractions points to hydrogen.

column9: Element Z has atomic number 16 and mass number 34. Which describes a neutral atom of Z?
column28: Atomic number 16 means 16 protons; neutral means 16 electrons; neutrons = 34 − 16 = 18. A common mistake is giving the extra 2 to electrons instead of neutrons, or using the mass number as the proton count.
column29: Atomic number gives protons; mass number − atomic number gives neutrons.

column9: Sample 1 contains only Cl₂ molecules. Sample 2 contains only HCl molecules. Which statement is correct?
column14: Both samples are compounds because both are made of molecules with two atoms each
column15: Sample 1 is an element and sample 2 is a compound, and both are made of molecules
column16: Sample 1 is a compound and sample 2 is an element, because Cl₂ has more atoms
column28: Cl₂ is two chlorine atoms bonded: a molecule of one element. HCl is hydrogen and chlorine bonded: a molecule that is a compound. A common mistake is calling every molecule a compound; a compound needs at least two different elements.
column29: Count the different elements in each formula.

column9: Which particles have MORE electrons than protons? Select all that apply.
column28: A negative charge means extra electrons, so Cl⁻, O²⁻, and F⁻ have more electrons than protons. K⁺ and Ca²⁺ have fewer electrons than protons, and neutral Ne has equal numbers. A common mistake is thinking the + sign means extra electrons.
column29: Extra negative particles give a negative charge.

column9: Carbon-14 slowly changes into nitrogen-14 when one of its neutrons turns into a proton. Why is the new atom nitrogen instead of carbon?
column14: Its mass number changed, and the mass number decides which element it is
column15: It now has 7 protons, and the number of protons decides the element
column17: It lost a neutron, so it is now just a lighter isotope of carbon
column28: Carbon has 6 protons. After a neutron becomes a proton, the atom has 7 protons, and every atom with 7 protons is nitrogen. The mass number stays 14 (one fewer neutron, one more proton). Students often think neutrons or mass decide the element.
column29: Count the protons before and after.

column9: Glycerol, a building block of fats, has the formula C₃H₈O₃. How many atoms in total are in 3 molecules of glycerol?
column28: One glycerol has 3 + 8 + 3 = 14 atoms. Three molecules have 3 × 14 = 42 atoms. A common mistake is counting only one molecule (14).
column29: Find the atoms in one molecule, then multiply by 3.

column9: A student draws four particle diagrams. Which drawing shows a compound made of molecules?
column14: Many single atoms, all the same kind, not touching
column15: Pairs of identical atoms bonded together
column16: Single atoms of two different kinds, mixed together but not bonded
column17: Groups that each have 1 large atom bonded to 2 smaller atoms of a different kind
column28: A compound made of molecules has different kinds of atoms bonded together in the same pattern, like the groups of 1 large atom and 2 smaller ones (similar to H₂O). Single identical atoms are an element, identical pairs are an element made of molecules, and unbonded atoms of two kinds are a mixture: the atoms are not bonded, so no compound formed.
column29: Look for two things at once: different kinds of atoms AND bonds between them.

column9: Atoms of the same element always have the same number of ___, but they can have different numbers of neutrons or electrons.
column28: The number of protons (the atomic number) identifies the element. Different neutrons make isotopes, and different electrons make ions, but the protons stay the same. A common mistake is answering electrons.
column29: Which number would turn the atom into a different element if it changed?

column9: A potassium ion, K⁺, and a neutral argon atom, Ar, both have 18 electrons. Potassium has 19 protons and argon has 18. Why are they different particles?
column14: They have different numbers of protons, so they are different elements
column15: They are isotopes of the same element
column16: They are the same particle because they have the same number of electrons
column17: K⁺ has extra electrons, which makes it heavier than the argon atom
column28: Electrons don't decide the element; protons do. K⁺ has 19 protons and Ar has 18, so they are different elements. K⁺ has one fewer electron than protons, so it is +1, while argon is neutral. Matching electrons does not make two particles the same.
column29: Compare protons, not electrons.

column9: Which statements are true of ALL compounds? Select all that apply.
column14: They are always made of ions
column15: They are always liquids at room temperature
column16: They contain two or more different elements
column17: Their elements are in a fixed ratio
column28: Every compound has two or more different elements, chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. Some compounds are ionic (NaCl) and some are covalent (H₂O), they can be solids, liquids, or gases, and many have no carbon (water, salt).
column29: For each statement, try to think of one compound that breaks it.

column9: A water molecule, H₂O, has 10 protons in total (8 from oxygen and 1 from each hydrogen). How many electrons does a neutral water molecule have?
column28: A neutral particle has equal protons and electrons, so 10 protons means 10 electrons. Bonding moves or shares electrons, but a neutral molecule keeps the same total. A common mistake is counting only the shared electrons in the bonds (4).
column29: Neutral means the charges balance.

column9: Your bones contain phosphate ions, written PO₄³⁻. What does the 3− tell you about this group of atoms?
column14: Altogether it has 3 fewer electrons than protons
column16: Altogether it has 3 more electrons than protons
column28: A charge of 3− means 3 extra electrons compared to protons across the whole group. Extra protons would make it positive, and the formula shows only 1 phosphorus atom (P with no subscript). A common mistake is reading the charge as a count of atoms.
column29: A negative charge always means extra electrons.
